profile: Opens a paragraph on the word or idea the last one ended with: 'That side of the religion is called ʿirfan.' -> 'ʿIrfan is the Arabic name for…'; '…a machine inside which is [rusted].' -> 'That machine is the soul.'; 'Repair is only the start.'
Ends paragraphs on the point itself, often on the Sheikh's own words, not on a tidy line: 'In most of us, he says, it is not working.'; 'it is a path that "has a beginning and no end".'

Medium sentences; two clauses joined by 'and' with no comma: 'ʿIrfan is the Arabic name for what English books call Islamic mysticism and the two words do not say the same thing.' Never chains three or more with 'and'.

Semicolon for a balanced contrast: 'A faculty that exists but has rusted can be repaired; one that is absent cannot be made fit for purpose.' Colon for a list or a gloss: 'The signs are all around us: in marriage, in the people we meet…'. 'whereas' once: 'Eyes and ears take in the surface of things, whereas inside a human being…'.

Names sources once per paragraph and varies the verb: 'Sheikh Bahmanpour reads it as', 'He compares', 'He adds', 'ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi explains', 'Imam Khomeini insists', 'In Murtada Mutahhari's words'. 'he says' appears at most once or twice per paragraph, parenthetically mid-sentence.

Quotations are short, inline, and always glossed in the following sentence: '"There is a machine inside which is [rusted]." That machine is the soul.'; '"what the signs indicate is not this world…". Most of us see only the lamp.'

Stance is 'we/us/most of us' with a rare 'you'; invites rather than lectures: 'Let's start with two claims.'; 'let's turn to the Qur'an'; 'We have heard these verses many times'. No scolding, no presuming what the reader feels.

Enumerated structure with plain markers and cross-references: 'The first is… The second is…'; 'as Chapter One shows'; 'the subject of this chapter'; 'Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences.'

Plain, concrete, written register with homely images: red light and lamp, rusted machine, 'getting them right', 'why a believer should bother'. Uses singular 'they' for the generic believer: 'provided they do what is wajib'.
Light hedging only where views differ ('this book presents each view with neutrality'); otherwise flat assertion: 'This claim is not contested.'
Never: rhetorical questions, aphoristic closers, intensifiers, 'So'/'Indeed' openers, paragraph-long recaps of what was just said, or and-and-and rhythm for effect.

tells: Picks up 'This knowledge…', semicolon contrast 'Such statements are true; each says what God is not', varied verbs ('he says', 'he grants'), cross-reference 'the subject of Chapter Four', quotations glossed afterwards.

'Let's start with the two kinds of knowing' mirrors A's invitation; second paragraph opens on the last one's term ('Acquired knowledge works by…'); 'Sheikh Bahmanpour draws the lesson from the word: to define a thing is to limit it' is A's colon-gloss; 'he adds' once.

'he says' five times in two paragraphs ('The first three ranks, he says', 'ordinary people, he says', 'It is difficult, he says', 'yet he says', 'A human being, he says') — Author A names the Sheikh once per paragraph and varies the verb (reads, compares, adds, insists)
'He means this as a statement of what we were made for.' — a gloss that restates the quotation without moving on; Author A glosses once and goes to the next step
'because we are made for it… what we were made for… God created us with that capacity and wants us to reach it' — three phrasings of the same point; Author A says a thing once

'Let's start with the order…', 'with which this book opened' cross-reference, comma dropped before 'and' ('being cut off and the Munajat asks for it complete'), the Sheikh's question reported and answered flatly ('In the heart, he answers, it is').
Opens on 'The severance…' from the last point, ties to 'Chapter One', and glosses the quotation immediately ('What the prayer asks to lose is the heart's love for the world, not the world itself').

'to see, in the marriage and the sleep and the rain, the One whose signs they are' — an and-and-and cadence and a capitalised flourish as a closing line; Author A ends on the point ('Most of us see only the lamp') and lists with commas

'The Qur'an is not asking for a new set of duties. It is asking whether we perceive what is already in front of us.' — a balanced antithesis as a paragraph close; Author A would state it once: 'The Qur'an asks us to perceive what is already in front of us'
'the same week in which he prays and fasts' — generic 'he'; Author A uses singular 'they' ('provided they do what is wajib')

'None of it is exotic.' / 'Here is the passage the wedding verse belongs to.' — presentational, slightly performative phrasing; Author A would write 'let's turn to the Qur'an and read on from the verse'

Enumerated 'The second gift… The third gift…' with a Sheikh gloss after each verse ('This good life, hayat tayyiba, is in Sheikh Bahmanpour's reading a clean life'); the single-sentence paragraph after the Surah Yunus verse is thinner than A's usual gloss, which keeps this near the middle.

'this, for Sheikh Bahmanpour, is how…' matches 'For Sheikh Bahmanpour, this is the whole subject'; semicolon contrast between mind-to-mind and heart-to-heart; second paragraph opens on 'This light'; 'the Sheikh adds' once.

'The prayers go on to ask for three things: … Let's take them in turn.' then 'The first is sight' is A's enumeration and invitation; 'Sheikh Bahmanpour explains why…' with the explanation following. The opener 'A heart cleared of everything but God is free for Him' is a little neater than A's habit.

'These words come near the end of Duʿa Kumayl… The line asks God for…' follows A's prayer-opening pattern; 'many of us hear it'; chapter cross-references ('the question Chapter Two ended on', 'This chapter sets out what those prayers ask for').

'For some of us, the Sheikh says…' with the prayer then glossed ('The prayer asks to be placed with these: among those…'); Mutahhari quoted with 'he writes' and explained afterwards ('He cites them to show that ʿirfan has its sources inside Islam').

Opens on the last paragraph's point ('Knowledge that analysis cannot produce has to come from somewhere else'); the hadith is glossed line by line with a semicolon ('The light is not gathered at all; God places it in the heart'); anticipates a misreading and hands to the next verse without a flourish.

'The scholars differ in emphasis but agree that powers are not the aim. Sheikh Bahmanpour calls such powers shirk. Mutahhari explains why seeking them would be so' — a whole paragraph recapping the two paragraphs above; Author A does not summarise what he has just said, he moves to the next step
'Murtada Mutahhari uses the same word as Sheikh Bahmanpour.' — withholds the word (shirk) until the end of the passage; Author A names the term at once ('That side of the religion is called ʿirfan')

'and he recalls Imam ʿAli (as) saying that he worshipped God not from fear of His Fire or desire for His Paradise but because he found Him worthy of worship' — a second, unrelated authority tacked on with 'and' to a sentence already carrying a quotation; Author A gives one source per sentence

Opens by picking up repair ('If the faculty can be repaired, there should be people in whom it already works'); colon list 'two groups: those whose souls work and those whose souls do not'; verse glossed with a semicolon pair and then handed on to the next verse.

Enumerates powers concretely ('to be in two places at once, to see the future or the past') and ends on the Sheikh's definition ('catching the signs of Allah: becoming sensitive to them and learning to hear and see'), as the reference does; the opening recap 'This is the case for pursuing ʿirfan' and the informal 'the real thing' hold it near the middle.

Semicolon contrast opener ('Other people look at the surface of the world; the friends of God look at what lies inside it'); 'Sheikh Bahmanpour is careful about what this means' then the qualification; 'The first gift is nearness:' enumeration; Arabic term given and glossed ('The Arabic for "brought near" is muqarrabun').

Each scholar named once, quoted briefly and glossed in the next sentence ('In his scheme, what is learned from the jurist begins the circle…'; 'His list starts with the heart and every item after it is a form of purification'); 'the third' keeps A's enumeration.

'shares its root with ʿilm al-huduri' echoes A's 'shares its root with maʿrifah'; quotation followed by a plain gloss ('A result in the laboratory is known because it has been observed, not because it has been deduced'); one source per paragraph, 'he reports', 'he writes'.
